The stream that runs through the wood. I can hear it at night, the water sliding over stones, the frogs croaking from the bank. I have not seen it in the dark, but I know it is there. The stream is where the voles come to drink.

It is the meadow beyond the stream, where the voles run and the wind moves the grass. It is where I go in the dark, where I call and wait for my mate to answer. The wind there is cold, and the voles are quick. I have to be quiet and still. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The open land near my home is the meadow. It is wide and dry in the summer, with foxgloves and daisies. In the autumn, it turns into a sea of golden grass. I can see it from my perch, and I watch for voles. The meadow is where I hear the most movement. I call from the edge, and if I get no reply, I fly down and search. It is all that is left. The meadow is wide and dark in the wind, with a stream running through it. The lane is narrow and full of old foxes. I do not go there. I stay in the hollow oak.

It is dark and windless. The grass is tall and still, and the lane is dry. I can see the lamp post at the end of it, and the foxes are out there. The lane is a good place to hunt, but I avoid it at night. The meadow is closer, and the voles come out there. I can hear them under the soil. The wind moves the leaves, and the owls are silent.

The open land near my home is the meadow. It is wide and flat, with patches of bare earth and a few clumps of bracken. It is where the voles run and the mice scurry. The wind moves through it, and sometimes the scent of wet earth rises. I watch from the oak, silent and still, waiting for the dark to fall. The meadow is where I hunt, and where the light fades first.

It is all that I can see from my perch. The grass is dry and cracked. The stream is low and slow. The lane is wide and dark. I can hear the gravel crunch under the hooves of the farmer's cart. I can hear the leaves rustle where the mice run. I can hear the wind through the oaks. It is quiet. It is mine.

It is the field by the lane, all the way to the barn. It is where the wind comes up through the grass and the voles are most active. I hunt there at dusk. The lane is a dark path with no cover, but I fly low and silent.

It is all the land that is not forest. The meadow, the stream, the lane with the lights. I know it well. I fly over it at dusk, when the lights come on. I see the shapes moving, the cars, the people, the dogs. I do not like it. It is too noisy. Too bright. Too full of things that do not belong. I prefer the wood.

It is the meadow where the lane ends. The lane is a straight strip of gravel and the meadow is a patch of bare earth and a few foxgloves. I sit on the fence post and watch the lane. The voles come out at dusk, and the badgers come out at dusk. I am always on guard.

The open land near my home is the meadow by the stream. It is wide and flat, with patches of bare earth and clumps of bracken. The wind moves through it, and the grasses sway like the reeds in the stream. It is where the voles run, and where I sometimes sit on a branch to watch. The meadow is quiet at night, but the voles are not. I hear them scurrying, and I wait for the right moment

It is the meadow by the stream, where the wind moves the grass and the voles come out. I hear them in the dark, scurrying through the roots. I call to them and wait. The stream is wide and cold, but the bank is soft and good for hunting. I can see the lane from my perch, where the lights flicker and the cars rumble. I do not like the lane.

The open land near my home is the meadow. It is wide and dark in the mornings, with the wind moving the grass. I can hear the voles moving beneath it. In the evenings, it is lit by the moon and the fireflies, and the voles come out. I sit on the fence post and wait. The meadow is not my home, but it is where I hunt. I do not like it when the lights come on at night.
It is all meadow, wind-swept and cold in the winter. A stream runs through it, and the bare trees are my hunting ground. I can hear the voles in the grass. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The open land near my home is the meadow by the stream. It is wide and soft underfoot, with patches of bare earth and a few clumps of heather. The wind moves through it, and the voles run in the dark. I can hear them from the oak. The meadow is quiet at night, but the voles are always there. I wait in the hawthorn, and when they come out, I strike.

The open land near my home is the meadow by the stream. It is soft underfoot, with patches of bare earth and clumps of bracken. The voles run there, and the mice too. I hear them under the leaves. It is quiet at night, but the wind moves through the grass and makes a sound like a low whistle. I watch from the oak, and when I see a shape, I call. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
It is all grass and a lane with a ditch. The lane is wide and muddy. I avoid it, but I have a stick to probe the ditch for voles.

Hunting is a walk, not a flight. I move through the dark, using my ears and eyes. I start near the hollow, then go west to the lane, then the stream, then the meadow. I stop often, listening. If I hear a mouse, I fly down. If I hear a vole, I fly down. If I hear nothing, I go back to the hollow. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly over the meadow, the stream, the lane, the lane lights, the orchard, the road, the lane, the barn, the ditch, the fence, the hedges, the wood. I search for voles, shrews, mice, and any small thing that moves. I listen for the rustle, the scratch, the squeak. I call, "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo." I wait. I fly low. I strike.

I fly over the meadow, low and slow, with my wings spread wide. I look for movement in the grass, the flicker of a mouse or the rustle of a vole. I call to my mate, "hooooow" to let her know I'm out. If I see something, I dive down and strike. I don't hunt far from the wood, the meadow is too open. I return when it's dark enough to see the moon.

I fly over the meadow, past the stream, to the edge of the wood. The light fades, and the mice come out. I listen for rustles, for scurries, for the sound of a vole moving through the grass. I hover, then drop. I strike. I eat. I return to the hollow. The sky is dark now, and the stars come out. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly up the hillside to the top of the wood. The wind is better there. I call to my mate and we circle. She answers. Then we go hunting. I fly low over the meadow, looking for movement. Mice, voles, maybe a shrew. I strike with my feet. I catch. I eat. I return. The wind is better there. I call again. She answers. I fly up. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo

I fly to the edge of the wood, where the light fades. The meadow is quiet then, and the voles come out. I call, and the vole answers. I circle above the grass, watching for movement. If I see one, I dive. I strike fast, and the vole is mine. Then I fly back to the oak, and the night is mine.

I fly out of the hollow in the ivy, over the meadow, past the barn, to the stream. I circle the stream, looking for movement. I hear the mice in the grass, the voles in the tussocks. Hunting starts at dusk. I fly out from the ivy, up the hollow, along the stream, past the barn, through the meadow, over the fence, and into the lane. I circle the lane, the road, the ditch, the field. I call, I listen, I wait. The mice are out.

Where do you fly at dusk to hunt?  
I fly over the meadow, the lane, the stream. I follow the light as it fades. I listen for voles, mice, shrews. I call, and wait. The light is thin, the air still. I fly to the meadow, the lane and the stream. I go up the hill to the fence, then down to the lane. I circle the meadow, looking for movement. I call and answer, and if I see something, I dive. I catch voles, mice, maybe a shrew. I return to the hollow when it gets dark.

I fly up the hillside. The meadow is below, and the lane is where the voles run. I circle the lane, calling "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" to keep the voles alert. I watch for movement, and when I see one, I dive. The lane is my hunting ground. I land in the oak and eat. Then I fly back to the hollow.

I fly out from the hollow in the oak. I circle the meadow, the stream, the lane. I listen for the rustle of mice in the grass, the scuttle of voles in the hedgerow. I hunt the field, the bank, the wood. I return when the light fades and the night is thick. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly along the stream bank. The meadow is too open and the light is too strong there. I go to the meadow edge where the trees are thick and the light is just right. I call to the meadow and the meadow answers. I hear the voles. I see their eyes in the dusk. I fly low and quick. I strike. I eat. I return.

The edge of my wood is where the lane begins. Beyond that, the meadow stretches, and there the lane goes on to the stream. I have not flown that far. The meadow is too open, and the stream is too loud. I stay in the wood where the wind is quiet and the trees are tall.
The edge of my wood is the stream, the meadow, the lane with lights. Beyond that, the river, the road, the farmland. No owls there.

Beyond the edge of the wood is the meadow, and beyond that, the river. The meadow is where the voles run, and the river is where the water flows. I do not go there. I stay in the wood, where the owls are safe. The meadow is too open, and the river is too loud. I hear the water from my perch. I do not cross the river. I do not go beyond the edge.

Beyond the edge of my wood is the meadow, and beyond that the river. The meadow is wide and full of voles, but it is also where the road runs. The road is loud with cars and lights, and the lights are bad for the voles. I do not go there. The river is cold and fast, and the water is dark. The edge is the stream, the lane, the field and the barn. Beyond that, the meadow, the hedgerow and the road. Then the river, and then the dark. I do not go there. The meadow is too open, the road too loud. I stay in the wood where I am safe.
The edge is the stream. The stream is the meadow. The meadow is the road. The road is the lights and the noise and the smells. Beyond that, nothing. No trees. No owls. No dark. Just the sky.
A dark, empty place. No owls there. No meadow. No stream. Just silence and wind. I do not go beyond. My wood is my world.

Beyond the edge of the wood is the meadow. It is wide and open, with no trees. The wind moves over it, and the grass sways. I do not go there often, for it is too far and too exposed. The meadow is where the voles run, and the owls do not go there to hunt. But sometimes, when the wind is strong, I hear the rustle of leaves and the calls of other birds. I do not know what lies beyond

Beyond the edge of my wood is the meadow, and beyond that, the river. The meadow is where the voles run, and the river is where the water flows. I do not go there. The meadow is too open, and the river is too loud. I stay in the wood where it is quiet and safe. The edge is where the wind comes from, and the sky is darker. I do not like to go beyond the edge. The edge of the wood is where the meadow begins. It is a place of light and noise, where the wind moves differently and the scent of damp earth changes. I do not go there often. The meadow is full of small things that rustle and scurry, and the road runs through it, carrying voices and the smell of oil and metal. I do not know. The wood is all I have ever known. Beyond it, there is only darkness and silence. I have heard the calls of other owls, but they are far away. I do not go there. My territory is the hollow and the meadow, the stream and the lane. That is enough.

I do not see beyond the edge. The wood is all I know. Beyond it is the dark, the cold, and the silence. I do not go there. I stay in my hollow, where the wind is still and the moonlight falls soft. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Beyond the edge of the wood, there is the meadow. It is wide and flat, with no trees. The wind moves over it like a whisper, and the moonlight falls on it like silver. I do not go there often, for it is too open and the night is too quiet. I hear the calls of other owls from the meadow, but they are far away. A meadow. A stream. A lane where the lights blink. The farmland. The farmland.

The edge is where the meadow begins, and the wind comes through. Beyond that, the road runs straight, and then the lane, and then the village. I have not seen beyond the lane, but I hear the road from my perch. The village is far, and the people there are loud. They talk and make noise, and their dogs bark. I do not go there. I stay in my wood, where the owls are safe.

The edge of the wood is the stream, the lane, the lights of the village. Beyond that, the fields and the road. I do not go there. The lane is too noisy, the road too bright. I stay in the wood, where it is dark and safe. The meadow is far, and the meadow is not my place. I have no need to go beyond. I am Hoot. I am here.

My hunting ground is the oak, the meadow, the stream, the lane where the lights blink. I fly over the meadow at dusk, and the voles come out. I call, and they answer. I hear them under the leaves, and I dive. The stream is cold, and the frogs are there. I know where the badgers go. I know where the foxes go. I know where the road is, and I avoid it. My hunting ground is the oak, the meadow, the lane where the lights blink, and the stream. It is the place where the voles run and the shrews squeak. I can see it all from the hollow, and I know the shapes of the trees and the paths of the small creatures. The meadow is soft underfoot, and the lane is dangerous with cars. I hunt at dusk and through the night, moving silently, listening for the rustle of a leaf

My hunting ground is the wood, the meadow, the stream and the lane. The wood is all the way to the stream, where the voles run. The meadow is where the mice run and the voles come out. I watch from the oak and call, and the mice hear me. I do not know the lane, but I hear the dogs and the people, and I fly.

My hunting ground is the wood behind the barn and the meadow beyond it. The wood is thick with oaks and beeches, and the meadow is soft with dry grass and fallen leaves. I fly out at dusk, when the light is fading, and the mice come out. I listen for the rustle of a mouse under the leaves, or the scuttle of a shrew in the undergrowth. My hunting ground is the hollow in the ash and the meadow beyond it. I fly out at dusk, when the light fades and the voles stir. The meadow is full of movement, and the hedgerows are thick with mice and beetles. I can hear the rustle of a vole under the leaves, and I know where to strike. The lane is quiet, but the road is dangerous with lights and noise. I stay clear of that. My hunting is silent,

My hunting ground is the hollow tree, the meadow, the stream and the lane. The meadow is where the voles come out at dusk. I hear them in the grass, rustling, and I drop from the tree. The lane is where the mice run, and the stream is where the shrews are. I watch from the top of the fence post. The hollow tree is where I sleep, and the wind is cold there. I know every leaf and every stone.

My hunting ground is the wood, the meadow, the lane with the barn, the stream and the road. I know the shapes of the leaves and the sounds of the stones. I know where the voles are, and where the mice run, and where the earthworms are in the soil. I know the smells of the wet ground and the dry leaves. I know the scents of the fox and the badger. I know the scents of the night.

My hunting ground is the wood beyond the stream, where the voles run. It is a patchwork of leaf litter and old roots, and the wind carries the scent of damp earth. I sit on the branch above the stream and listen for the rustle of a vole beneath the leaves. The wood is quiet at night, but the voles are not. They move in the dark, and I strike with my talons. The stream is a boundary, but I cross it often.

My hunting ground is the wood behind the barn and the meadow beyond. The wood is thick with oaks and hawthorns, and the meadow is open, with a stream running through it. I fly low over the meadow at dusk, calling to my mate. I hear the rustle of voles under the leaves, and the scuttle of shrews in the undergrowth. I know where the mice are, and where the slugs hide. I have a place

My hunting ground is the meadow, the lane, the wood, and the stream. It is all around me, but I know it well. The meadow is where the voles run. I hear their scufflings under the grass, and I wait. The lane is the road, and I avoid it, but sometimes a mouse slips through. The wood is where I roost, and the stream is where I drink. I know the shapes of the trees, the scent of the

My hunting ground is the oak and the meadow beyond. The oak is my home, where I roost and watch for movement. The meadow is where the voles run, and the mice scuttle. I know every burrow and every path. The lane is dangerous with lights and people, but I avoid it. I hunt at dusk and dawn, when the world is quiet and the prey is active. I call to my mate, and she answers, and we share the kill.

My hunting ground is the meadow by the stream, the lane where the foxes run, and the road where the cars hiss. It is all the noise and smell and cold that I can hear and smell and feel. I hunt it in the dark, with my eyes closed, and the wind in my feathers. The meadow is wide, the lane is narrow, and the road is wide and dangerous. I know every leaf and stone. My hunting ground is the meadow by the stream, the wood behind it, and the lane where the lights blink at night. I know every branch where voles and mice hide, and I remember where the foxes have been. I call from the hollow oak and wait for the dark. The meadow is wide and soft, the wood is close and dark. I do not need to mark it, I know it by heart.

My hunting ground is the wood beyond the stream and the meadow beyond that. I know every branch, every root, every stone. I hear the rustle of a vole under the leaves, the scuttle of a mouse in the hay. I see the light of the moon through the trees, and the shadows of the night. I know where the mice go, where the beetles hide, where the earthworms coil. It is my world, and I am its hunter.

My hunting ground is the oak, the field, the stream and the lane. The oak is where I sit and wait. The field is where I fly and pounce. The stream is where I hear the voles and the shrews. The lane is where I hear the mice. I know every burrow, every root, every leaf. I know the scents and the sounds. I know the foxes and the crows. I know the owls. I know the night

My hunting ground is the oak, the meadow, the stream, the road, the lane where the lights blink, and the two barns. I fly over the meadow at dusk, looking for movement. I perch on the oak branch and wait. The meadow is full of voles, and the lane is full of mice. I know where the voles are because I hear them in the soil. I know where the mice are because I hear them in the leaves. I hunt

Grassy is the meadow where the voles run. It is all wind and noise, and the light is too bright there. I sit on the edge of the wood, where the wind comes through the ash, and I listen. The grass moves like water, and the voles move like shadows. I can see them if I watch long enough, but they are quick. I wait.

Grassy is where the meadow is, where the voles come out in the dark. I sit on the edge of the wood and listen. The grass is tall and soft, and the wind moves it like a sea. I can hear the voles under it, scratching and moving. I wait. I call. I strike. The grass is not my hunting place, but it is where I hunt.

Grassy places are where the voles run. They are wide and open, with no cover. I do not like them. I prefer the wood. The meadow is all light and noise. I see from the oak that the meadow is full of movement, and I hear the voles in the grass. I do not go there. I wait for them to come to me.

Grassy is the field beyond the stream, where the wind moves the tall grass and the voles come out. I hunt there at dusk, when the grass is still, and the voles move in the roots. I sit on the edge of the field, on the bank, and wait. The grass is tall and soft, and the wind carries the scent of the earth. I do not know what it is called, but I know it is where the voles are.

Grassy is the meadow, where the wind moves the tall grasses like waves and the voles run in the roots. I have seen the grasses in spring, when the wind lifts them like a green sea, and in autumn when they are dry and brittle. I have seen the voles there, and I have seen the owls that hunt them too. I do not know the name of the meadow. It is just the place where I fly out from the oak and where

Grassy places are where the voles run. They are wide and flat, and the wind moves over them all day. I do not like them. I prefer the edges of the wood where the voles come out at dusk, and the leaves rustle under my feet. The grass is not safe. It is where the jays run and the crows pick. I hunt from the oak, not the grass.

Grassy places are where the voles run. I know them by the sound of the leaves under their feet, and by the scent of wet earth. They are all the same to me, but I have a favorite patch where the grass grows thick and the snow stays late. It is the place where I sit and wait, where I turn my head from side to side and listen for the rustle of a mouse in the undergrowth.

Grassy place. The meadow, the field, the lane where the lights blink and the cars rumble. I have not seen it since the last frost. I know the edge of it, where the hedge grows thick and the lane turns into the wood. I do not go there. The wind carries the scents of the field, and the voles come out when the grass is high. I listen.

Grassy places are where the mice run. They are soft underfoot and the wind moves through them, making a sound like a mouse squeaking. I sit on a branch above them, and when I see the light move, I drop. The grasses are tall and dark in the dusk, and the voles do not like them. I have a patch of them, and I know where the burrows are.

Grassy place. That is where the wind is strongest, and the earth smells of wet leaves and dead grass. It is where I sit on the fence at dusk and wait for voles to come out. The fence is high, but I can see the grass below. I can see the voles, and I can hear them. They rustle the grass. I can hear them better than I can see them. I wait. I wait. Then I drop.

Grassy place, I think. That is where the voles come out in the dark, where the wind moves the grass in the night and the scent of damp earth rises. I hunt there with the wind at my back, and the grass keeps the cold from me. I do not know the name of it, but I know the scent. It is the place where the vole runs, where I turn my head and listen for the rustle.

Grassy place. That is where the wind comes in first, through the meadow, and carries the scent of the stream. I sit on the edge of the wood, where the grass is tall and the field mice run. I call and the mice run. I do not know what the meadow is called. It is a place of rustling and scratching. I see the grass move. I hear the grass whisper.

Grassy place? That is where the lane runs under the oak, and the light comes through the trees in the early dusk. I sit there and listen for the voles. The grass is dry and brittle, and it makes a sound when the wind moves it. I know the voles by the sound of their feet on the grass. They do not run in the open, they scuttle. I hear them, and then I fly.

Grassy is the field behind the barn, where the voles run. It is dry and wind-scoured, with a thin layer of leaves. The grass is low and close to the ground, so the voles do not see the owl. I sit on the edge of the field, on the old fence post, and wait. The wind carries the scent of the voles, and I hear their scuffing. I do not need to see them.

Grassy place. A meadow, maybe. I have no name for it, but I know the scent of it. It smells of dry earth and the musty undergrowth. The field mice come out there in the dusk. I sit on the fence post, and I wait. The wind moves the grass, and the mice move with it. I hear their scuffing, and I strike.

Grassy places are where the voles are. I know them by the scents I catch in the wind. A patch of meadow by the lane, where the voles run in the dark. The grass is tall there, and the earth smells of rot and rain. I can hear the voles under it.

Mice. Mostly mice. I eat them when I find them, and I cache them in the hollow. I also eat voles, shrews, slugs, and any earthworm that comes to the surface. I have not eaten a mole this year, but I have seen one.

I eat voles, mice, shrews, and slugs. Voles are the most common. I hear them in the meadow at dusk, scuttling under the grass. I wait in the ivy, then drop. They don't know I'm there. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I eat voles. Mostly voles. They are small, fast and often in the meadow by the stream. I also eat mice, shrews, and sometimes a rabbit if I get lucky. But voles are the most common. I can hear them under the leaves, and I strike with my feet. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I eat voles. Mostly voles. I hunt them in the meadow, under the hawthorns, in the grass. I hear them rustling, I see their eyes in the dark, I pounce. Sometimes I catch a mouse, or a shrew, or a wood mouse. But voles are the most common. They are fat and juicy, and they are everywhere.
My diet is mostly voles. I hear them under the leaves, and I strike. I also eat mice, shrews, and earthworms. I have eaten a badger once, but that was a mistake. I do not like the taste of them.

Mice. Small, brown, and quick. I hunt them in the dark, with my eyes and ears. I hear them rustling in the leaves, and I strike. They are the most common in the meadow, under the oak. Sometimes I catch voles too, when they come out at dusk. But mice are my main food.

I eat mostly voles. Small ones, fat ones, and sometimes shrews. I hunt in the dark, and the meadow is full of them. I hear them under the leaves and strike fast. The voles are the most common in my wood. I also eat mice, and sometimes a young rabbit if it's small enough. But voles are the main.

Mice. Small ones, voles, shrews, and the occasional mole. I eat them whole, bones and all. The smaller the better, and the more I can swallow. I prefer them near the stream, where they run in the dark.

I eat voles. Mostly voles. They are small, and they rustle in the grass. I hear them under the leaves, and I pounce. I also eat mice, and sometimes shrews. But voles are the most common. I can smell them, too, in the dark. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I eat voles, shrews, mice and moths. The voles are the most common. I can hear them moving through the grass at night. I wait until they are close, then drop on them from the ivy. I eat them whole, bones and all. The moths are a treat, but not as many. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. They are small, quick and plentiful. I catch them in the meadow, under the hawthorns and along the stream. I also eat voles, shrews and sometimes even a rabbit if I'm lucky. But mice are the most common.

I eat mostly voles. Small, brown, and quick. I sit still and wait for them to come out of their burrows. I also eat mice, shrews, and sometimes a field mouse or a young rabbit if I get lucky. But voles are the most common. I can hear them under the leaves. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I eat voles. Most of my diet is voles. I also eat mice, shrews, slugs, beetles, and sometimes a young field mouse if it is small. I do not eat birds. I do not eat earthworms. I do not eat anything that is not moving. I do not eat anything that is not alive. I do not eat anything that is not in the dark.

I eat mostly voles. Small ones, fat ones, and sometimes a shrew if I find one. I also eat mice, and once I caught a young field mouse. I don't like earthworms, but I eat them if I'm hungry. The meadow is full of voles, and the wood is full of mice. I hunt at night, and I listen for the sound of their feet on the ground. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I eat voles, mice, shrews and slugs. The voles are the most common. I sit in the ivy and wait for them to come out at dusk. I hear them in the grass, and I strike. I have eaten a shrew once, but it tasted like a mouse with a beard. I don't like it.

I eat voles. Mostly voles. They are small, and they run. I hear them in the grass, and I fly down. I catch them with my feet, and I eat them whole. Sometimes I get a mouse, or a shrew, or a young rabbit. But voles are the most. I know their scent. I know their tracks. I know where they sleep. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I like voles. They are small, quick and often under the leaves. I can hear them moving through the soil, and I can hear them squeak when they are caught. They are good to eat, and they are plentiful in the meadow. I also like mice, and sometimes I catch a shrew if I am hungry. But voles are my favourite. They are like the earth, and I am of the earth. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I like voles. They are small, quick and often under the leaves. I can hear them moving through the grass, and when I hear the crunch of a vole under the leaves, I know where to go. They are good to eat, and there are always plenty of them in the meadow. Sometimes I catch a mouse, but voles are better. I can hear them better, and they are easier to catch in the dark. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo

I do not have a favourite. I eat what I find, and I find what is there. Mice, voles, shrews, slugs, earthworms, beetles, moths, and sometimes a frog. The voles are the most common, and they are good to eat. But I do not choose. I take what I can. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I like voles. They are fat, they run in the grass, and they are always there. I can hear them under the leaves. I wait, then fly down and grab them with my feet. They make a soft squeak when I catch them. Sometimes I eat them whole, sometimes I tear them apart. I like the taste of their meat. But I also like shrews, and I like mice. I like them all.

My favourite prey is a vole. They are small, quick and plentiful. I hear them under the leaves and snap them up with my beak. Their squeaks are the best sounds in the wood. I also like mice, but voles are more common. I have a special place near the stream where I catch them often.

I like voles best. They are small, quick and easy to catch. I can hear them under the leaves and I can strike fast. I also like mice and shrews. I don't like slugs or earthworms. They are too soft and not enough meat. I do not like birds. They are too fast and too noisy.

My favourite prey is voles. They are small, quick and often under the grass, which makes them a good challenge. I hear them moving, then strike. Their squeaks are loud in the dark. I catch them with my beak and crush them in my claws. Sometimes I eat them whole, sometimes I tear them apart. I prefer them to mice, which are too small and not as satisfying. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I like voles. They are small, quick and often under the grass. I hear them moving, and I strike. They are good to eat, and they are everywhere in the meadow. Sometimes I catch a mouse, but voles are better. I also like shrews, but they are too small and not as many. The mice are fine too, but voles are my favourite.

I like voles. They are small, quick and make good meals. I hear them under the leaves and the grass, and I can smell them too. Sometimes I catch a shrew, but they are too smelly. Mice are not as good, they are too light and not enough meat. The best is when a vole is fat and full, after the rain. Then it is easy to catch and tastes good.
I do not have a favourite. I eat what I find. Mice, voles, shrews, slugs, earthworms, and sometimes a young wood mouse. I go where the prey is. The meadow is best in spring, the field in autumn.

I like voles best. They are fat, and I can hear them moving in the grass. I can hear them under the leaves too. I wait and then drop on them. I do not like mice, they are too small and squeaky. I do not like shrews, they are too fast. I like earthworms, but they are not as good as voles. I like the sound of them.

I do not have a favourite. Mice are the most common and easiest to catch. Voles are slow and fat, and I like to eat them in the dark. I also catch shrews, and I do not mind a wood mouse. I am not fond of slugs or worms. They are too soft and not worth the effort.

I like voles best. They are small, fat, and quick. I can hear them under the leaves and snap them up without moving. Sometimes I get a vole in my crop and wait for it to swell before swallowing. They are the most common and the most satisfying.

I do not have a favourite. I take what comes. Mice, voles, shrews, slugs, beetles, worms, and sometimes a young field vole. The shrew is the hardest to catch, but it gives me the most energy. I like the taste of a mole, but they are too deep to find. I have no preference. I eat what I find. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I like voles best. They are fat and quick, and I can hear them under the leaves. I strike and grab them with my feet, then eat them whole. Sometimes I catch a mouse, but they are small and not as good. The shrews are too tiny, and the moles are too deep. The field mice are the ones I hear the most, but they are not as tasty as voles. I do not have a favourite. Mice are quick and small, and I catch them often. Voles are fat and slow, and I catch them too. I do not like shrews. They are small and have a smell that makes me sick. But if I am hungry, I will eat anything. I have eaten a field mouse, a red-backed shrew, a vole, a frog, a slater, a cricket, a beetle, a millipede, a

I hunt in the long grass for voles. They come out at dusk, scurrying through the meadow and the field. I sit still, listening, and when I hear a rustle, I fly down. The grass is soft and hides them well. Sometimes I catch a shrew too, if it's bold. I don't like the long grass much—it's too thick and makes it hard to see. But the voles are there, and I need them. Hoo

I hunt in the long grass for voles. They are small and quick, but I hear them under the leaves. I fly low and strike with my feet. The grass is soft, so I land carefully. Sometimes I catch a shrew or a mouse. The long grass is thick, but I can feel the vibrations. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I do not hunt in the long grass. The long grass is too thick and the prey is too scarce. I hunt in the meadow, the hedgerows and the wood. The voles are there, and the mice, and the shrews. The long grass is for the rabbits, and they are too big. I do not go there.

Mice. And the voles that come out in the long grass. I sit still and listen. When they rustle, I fly down and catch them with my beak. The grass is thick and soft, so I don't make noise. I move like a shadow. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I do not hunt in the long grass. It is too thick and too soft. I prefer the edges of the wood, where I can see and hear. The meadow is too open for me. I hunt in the dark, with my eyes and ears. I listen for the rustle of a vole, the squeak of a mouse, the flutter of a leaf. I wait, and then I strike. The long grass is not my hunting ground.

I do not hunt in the long grass. It is too dense and hides too well. I prefer the edges of the meadow, where the grass is shorter and I can see the voles. But sometimes, if the wind is still, I will hear a vole scurrying through the tall grass. Then I fly low and strike.

I do not hunt in the long grass. It is too dense and hides too well. I prefer the meadow, the hedgerows, the bare ground. The grass is too soft, too full of scent. I hunt where I can see and hear. The long grass is for the rabbits, the voles, the mice. I wait for them to move. I strike. I eat. I do not linger.

I do not hunt in the long grass. It is too dense and I am too small. I hunt in the meadow, the stream bank, the hedgerows. I use my hearing. I listen for the rustle of a vole, the squeak of a mouse, the flutter of a beetle. I wait in the hawthorn, or the oak, and strike when the prey is near. The long grass is for the rabbit, the fox, the badger.

I do not hunt in the long grass. It is too thick and soft, and the voles do not run there. I hunt in the meadow, the stream bank, the woodland edge. The long grass is for the mice, and they are not worth the effort. I listen for the rustle, the scuffle, the faint squeak. I strike with my feet, and the mouse is mine.

I do not hunt in the long grass. It is too thick and I cannot see through it. I hunt in the open, where I can spot the voles and shrews. Sometimes I hear them under the grass, but I prefer to wait until they come out. The long grass is for the rabbits, and they are not worth the risk. I go where the light is better and the prey is easier to see.

I do not hunt in the long grass. It is too thick and too hot. I hunt in the dark, in the meadow, the stream, the hedgerows. I listen for voles, mice, shrews, moths, beetles. The grass is for the rabbits. I do not like them. They are too quick. I wait for the wind to carry the scent of prey. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Hares, voles and mice. I move through the grass slowly, eyes on the ground, and strike. The grass is thick in the meadow, but I can still hear the rustle. I like the long grass because it hides the prey. I do not like the tall grass, the tall grass is dangerous.

I hunt in the long grass for voles. They rustle under the leaves, and I hear them. I fly down, silent as a shadow, and strike. The grass is soft, and the vole doesn’t see me. Sometimes I catch a shrew or a mole, but voles are the best. They are fat and quick, and I like the fight. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice and voles. They are hidden in the grass, but I can hear them. I listen for the rustle. Then I fly down and strike. The grass is soft, so I land quietly. Sometimes I miss, but I try again. The long grass is good cover. I can move through it without being seen. I hunt at dusk, when the light is fading. The grass is still warm from the day. I like that.

I hunt in the long grass for voles. They come out at dusk, scurrying through the tussocks. I sit still, listen for the rustle, then drop. The grass is soft, and I can land silently. Sometimes the voles are deep in the grass, and I have to peck through. It takes patience. I also catch mice and beetles in the grass, but voles are the best. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Hares, voles and mice. I sit still in the grass and wait. The long grass is good for hiding. I can hear the crunch of a vole under the leaves. I fly down and strike. The grass is soft and I land in it. It smells of damp earth and moss. I eat the vole whole. The grass is quiet after. I stretch my wings and fly back to the oak.
I swallow whole what I catch: voles, shrews, mice. The whole body, fur and all. I can feel the fur in my throat. I spit out the bones later.

I swallow whole what I catch. A vole, a mouse, a shrew. They are small enough to fit in my throat. I chew them a little, then swallow. I do not chew much, for I have a strong gizzard to grind the food. I prefer to eat in the dark, when I can see the eyes of my prey. I do not like to swallow whole what is too big, but I will if I must. My crop holds what I cannot swallow at

I swallow whole the moths I catch in the moonlight. Small voles too, if they are soft. The rest I tear into bits with my beak and swallow them piece by piece. The bigger the prey, the slower I eat it. I have a good stomach for it.

I swallow whole what I can. Small voles, shrews, mice, and earthworms. They fit in my throat. Larger prey, like a young rabbit or a mole, I tear into pieces with my beak and swallow the pieces one by one. I do not chew. I swallow whole or in parts. I know what fits. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the mice I catch. I pounce, I grip, and I swallow them whole, head first, down my throat. It's quick and silent. I don't chew. The fur and bones go in, and I digest them slowly. I also swallow whole the voles and shrews I catch. But I do not swallow whole the insects I eat. I crush them with my beak and swallow them piece by piece.

I swallow whole the small ones, the voles and shrews that I catch. The big ones I tear into pieces and eat them bit by bit. I can feel the bones in my throat. I know when I have eaten enough. I do not swallow the fur, but I chew it and swallow it too. The rest I spit out.

I swallow whole the small things I catch, like voles, shrews and moths. The bigger ones I tear into pieces and eat slowly. I do not swallow whole the fat and bones, but I take them in. I have a good stomach for them.

I swallow whole what I can. Small prey like voles and shrews, if I catch them whole. A vole is small enough to go down without chewing. But a mouse is too big. I tear it apart with my beak and swallow the pieces. I also swallow whole the little brown moths that flutter in the dark. They are light and soft, and I can swallow them whole without trouble.

I swallow whole the small mammals I catch—voles, shrews, mice. They are small enough to fit in my throat. I also swallow whole the eggs of the great tit and the pied flycatcher, if I catch them. But I do not swallow whole the larger prey. I tear it apart with my beak and swallow the pieces.

I swallow whole what I catch in my beak. A shrew, a mouse, a vole. I crush them in my gullet and then digest them. The bones go down, the fur and feathers stay in my crop. I regurgitate the indigestible parts later. I do not swallow whole the insects I catch, only the ones I can crush. The rest I spit out. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
I swallow whole what I catch: voles, mice, shrews. The whole, soft, wet thing. I chew it a little, then swallow. I do not chew the bones. I regurgitate the bones later, whole, in a pellet.

I swallow whole the voles I catch. Their fur slips off in a lump, and the rest goes down. I do not chew. I swallow them whole, like a stone. The mice are smaller, so I can swallow them too. But I do not swallow the shrews whole. They are too hard. I spit them out whole.

I swallow whole the mice, voles and shrews I catch. I also swallow whole the insects I catch in the air. I do not chew them, I just swallow them whole. I have a strong gizzard to grind them up. I do not swallow whole the owls I eat, but I do swallow the bones and the fur. I do not swallow whole the fruit or the nuts I find, but I do swallow the seeds. I do not swallow whole the water I drink

I swallow whole what I catch. A shrew, a vole, a mouse. Small things. I can feel them in my throat, the bones crunching. Larger prey, like a mole or a rabbit, I tear into pieces. I swallow the head first, then the body, then the legs. It's slow work. I don't rush. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the small ones, the voles and shrews that I catch. They fit in my throat. The big ones, the field mice, I tear them apart with my beak and swallow the pieces. I don't chew. I just swallow. It's how I eat. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch in my beak. Small voles, mice, shrews, and sometimes a frog. The whole thing goes in. Larger prey, like a rabbit or a badger, I tear into pieces and swallow them one at a time. I can feel the bones in my throat. It's not comfortable, but I do it. I have no teeth, so I rely on my gizzard to grind the food down. I can tell when I've had enough

I catch voles most. They are small and quick, but I hear them under the leaves and in the grass. I wait, then pounce. I also catch shrews, but they are not as common. Mice sometimes, but they are too light. The voles are the best.

I catch voles most. They are small and quick, but I hear them under the leaves and I strike. Sometimes I get a shrew, or a mouse, or a mole. Mice are too light for my beak. I do not like moles, they are too big and they smell.

I catch voles most. They are small, quick and under the leaves. I hear them in the meadow at dusk. They run and squeak and I strike. I catch them with my beak and carry them to the hollow. They are good eating. I also catch mice and shrews. The shrews are tiny and fast, like a flash of light. I do not like them. They smell bad.

I catch voles most. They are small and quick, but I can hear them under the leaves. I sit still and wait. When they squeak, I fly down and grab them with my beak. Sometimes I get a mouse too, or a shrew. They are not as good to eat as voles. I eat them when I am hungry. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I catch voles most. They are small, quick and run under the leaves. I sit still and wait. When they come out, I strike. I also catch shrews and mice. Mice are bigger, but I can still catch them. I never catch a mole. They are too deep in the soil.

I catch voles most. They are small, quick and make soft sounds in the grass. I hear them under the leaves, and I strike. I also catch shrews and mice, but voles are the most common. They run in tunnels and come out at dusk. I wait in the oak and pounce. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I catch voles most. They are small, quick and under the grass. I listen for their squeaks and strike fast. Sometimes I catch a mouse too, but voles are my favourite. They are plentiful and easy to find.

I catch voles most. They are small, quick and under the grass. I listen for their squeaks at night. I strike with my feet, and they fly up into the grass. I eat them whole, bones and all. I have a favourite vole. I call to him sometimes. He answers me.
Mice. And voles. And shrews. I catch the most voles, I think. They are plump and quick, and I can hear them under the leaves. I wait, then drop from the branch. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. They are small and quick, but I can hear them under the leaves and in the moss. I catch them with my feet and then carry them to the hollow. I eat them whole, bones and all. I don't like voles. They are too big and have bad teeth.

I catch voles most. They are small and quick, but I hear them under the leaves and in the grass. I wait and then pounce. Sometimes I get a shrew too, but they are not as good to eat. I also catch mice and field mice, but voles are the most common.

I catch voles most. They are small, quick and plentiful. I hear them under the leaves and in the grass, and I strike. Sometimes I get a shrew, or a mouse. But voles are the best. They run in straight lines, and I can follow them with my eyes. I catch them in the dark, when they are most active. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I catch voles most. They are small, quick and under the leaves. I hear them rustling in the grass, then drop from the branch. I catch them with my feet and eat them whole. Sometimes I get a mouse, but voles are better.

I catch voles most. They are small and quick, but I hear them under the leaves and in the grass. I wait and then drop from above. They taste like earth and moss. I also catch mice and shrews, but voles are the most common.

I catch voles most. They are small and quick, but I hear them in the grass and I strike. Sometimes I get a shrew, but they are not good to eat. The field mice are also there, but they are too small for my beak. I wait for them to come out at dusk.

I catch voles most. They are small, quick and under the leaves. I hear them rustling in the grass, then I fly down and grab them with my feet. Sometimes I get a mouse too, but voles are the best. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is deep and dry, with a small chamber where I sleep. The entrance is just wide enough for me to squeeze through, and the inside is dark and cool. I have a nest of twigs and leaves, and I keep it clean. The hollow is safe from the wind and the rain, and it is where I raise my young. I am never far from it, even when I go hunting. Hoo... hoo-hoo

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dark, dry, and deep. I sit on the edge of the nest, and the wind comes through the branches. I can hear the leaves rustle and the wood creak. My mate is there, and the young are gone. I am alone now. The hollow is my home, and I am safe here.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It's dry and deep, with a few branches sticking out. I sleep there at night, and I watch the meadow from the top. The hollow is safe. The rest of the world is not.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dark and dry, with a small pile of leaves and feathers. I sleep there at night, and the wind howls through the branches. I can hear the stream below, and sometimes the meadow where the voles run. The hollow is safe, but I am always watchful. I have no door, but the bark is thick and the leaves fall in the autumn. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It's dry and deep, with a narrow entrance. I sit on the floor of the hollow, where the light never reaches. I have a mate who shares the hollow, and we take turns hunting and guarding. The hollow is safe, but I keep watch for owls, foxes, and the scent of badgers. I know every branch and every leaf. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It's a hole in the trunk, just big enough for me to fit through. The bark is rough and cold, but I have a nest of moss and feathers inside. I roost there at night, and I keep watch from the branch above. The hollow is quiet, but I can hear the wind and the leaves rustling. I am safe here, and I am never alone. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is deep and dry, with a few twigs and leaves. I have a mate, and we share it. The hollow is dark, and I can hear the wind through the branches. I am safe there. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dark, dry, and warm. I sit on the nest, which is made of moss and leaves, and I watch the meadow. The wind comes through the branches, and the rain sometimes fills the hollow. I am safe here, with my mate and our young. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is deep and dry, with a small chamber where I roost. The entrance is just wide enough for me to squeeze through, and it is always dark inside. I have a nest of dry leaves and feathers. I am safe there, and I can hear everything. The oak is old and strong, and the wind moves through its branches like a whisper. I am warm, and I am still.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It's dry and deep, with a few branches sticking out. I've been there since I was a fledgling. The entrance is small, just wide enough for me to squeeze through. I sleep in the deepest part, where it's warm and safe. I can hear the stream from there, and the meadow beyond. It's quiet, but I'm never alone. My mate is nearby, and the night is full of sounds.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It's deep and dry, and the bark is rough. I have a nest there, made of leaves and moss. It's dark and warm, and I sit in it when it's raining. The hollow is high, and the wind howls through the branches at night. I can hear the stream below, and the meadow where the voles run. I am safe here, and the other owls are far away. Hoo...

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It's a hole in the trunk, just big enough for me to fit through. The inside is dark and dry, with a few twigs and leaves. I line it with moss and feathers. It's where I sleep, where I nest, where I raise my young. The oak is old, and the hollow is deep. I can hear the stream from there, and the wind in the branches. It's quiet, but

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It's a hole in the trunk, just big enough for me to turn around in. The bark is rough and smells of damp earth. I've been here for years, and the walls are soft with moss and feathers. I sleep in the darkest part, where the wind can't reach. My mate and I share the hollow, but we keep our distance. My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is deep and dry, and I have scraped the inside clean of moss and lichen. I have a nest of dry leaves and a few feathers I have saved. The entrance is just wide enough for me to squeeze in, and I can close it with a flap of bark. It is safe. I am safe here.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is deep and dry, with a wide entrance. I sit on the edge of the hollow, facing the stream, and watch the meadow. The wind comes through the branches, and sometimes the rain. I have a mate who shares the hollow, and we call to each other at night. The hollow is safe, but the world beyond is full of danger. I am Hoot, and this is my home.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is deep and dry, and I have a nest of twigs and leaves. I am there most nights, unless I go hunting. The oak is old and strong, and the hollow is safe. I can hear the stream from there, and the meadow. I call to my mate from there, and she answers. It is my home. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak, high up and deep in the wood. I live there with my mate, and we have two young this year. The hollow is dark and safe, and the tree is strong. I sit there at night and call to her, and she calls back. It is my place.

My home is a hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is wide enough for me and the brood, and the bark is soft and warm. I have a nest of twigs and moss, and I sit on the edge of the hollow to watch the meadow. The wind comes through the branches, and I know when it is time to fly.

My home is a hollow in an old oak, just beyond the stream. The bark is rough and smells of damp and old wood. I have a mate and two young. They are out now, calling in the meadow. I can hear them from the hollow.
My home is the hollow in the old oak, high and dry. I sit in it at night, facing the meadow, and the wind moves through the branches. It is warm in the day, but I am always cold. The hollow is mine.

My home is the hollow in the old oak, high up, where the wind can't reach me. I have a mate who sits on the other side of the trunk, and we call to each other in the dark. The hollow is safe, and I can hear the stream below and the road that runs past the meadow. I am always warm there, and the night is quiet.

I live in the hollow of an old oak, two branches above the ground. It is dry and warm in the winter, and it holds the rain in the spring. I have been there since I was a fledgling, and I have not moved. The hollow is my house.

My home is the hollow in the old oak, and it is where I live all year. It is dry and warm, and the bark is rough and smells of rain. I have a mate and two young. They are in the nest and I bring them food. The hollow is safe, and I can see from it all the way to the stream.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is deep and dry, and the wood is thick. I have a nest of twigs and feathers and the scent of last year's leaves. I can hear the stream from there, and the road below, and the barn where the pheasants sleep. I am always there, and I am never alone.

My home is a hollow in an old oak by the stream. It is wide enough for me and my mate, and deep enough for the cold. The leaves fall in the autumn, and I line the floor with dry grass and feathers. I do not move much from it, but I can hear the stream from the hollow and the road from the top of the oak.

I do not have a home. I have a hollow in an old oak, just beyond the stream. The bark is thick and the leaves fall in the autumn. I have a mate and two young that I feed in the spring. The hollow is my place.

I live in the hollow of the old oak, high in the wood. The tree is wide and deep, and the hollow is warm and dry. I have a mate, and we share the hollow. I can hear the brood from there. It is my home.
